## Information

This page is a rework of a project completed for PSTAT 274 (Time Series
Analysis) at the University of California Santa Barbara, taught by Prof. Raya
Feldman (Spring 2023). The code behind every figure and table is available in
the "Show code" blocks.

**Abstract.** We select and fit a Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving
Average (SARIMA) model to produce accurate five year ahead forecasts of
atmospheric CO$_2$ levels above Mauna Loa, Hawaii. We investigate the
properties of the series, the suitability of SARIMA models, and whether the
forecasts capture future observations. The analysis uses exploratory
analysis, model selection with the adjusted Akaike Information Criterion
(AICc), diagnostic checking, residual analysis and spectral analysis. Our
first choice model, a SARIMA(0,1,3)(0,1,1)$_{12}$, produced approximately
Gaussian white noise residuals and accurate forecasts whose confidence
intervals captured the true observed values.

## Introduction

Many geophysical time series contain seasonal variation. A key example is
atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO$_2$) concentration, which has an annual
seasonal cycle - largely due to plant photosynthesis and respiration -
superimposed on an increasing trend caused primarily by human CO$_2$
production.

We examine monthly measurements of atmospheric CO$_2$ above Mauna Loa, Hawaii
over the 32 years from 1959 to 1990 [@brockwell1996; @shumway2011]. The aim is
a 5 year ahead forecast from a suitable SARIMA model. The workflow is:

- **Exploratory analysis:** decomposition, stationarity transformations,
  autocorrelations and tests for normality and stationarity.
- **Model fitting and selection:** stationarity and invertibility checks,
  coefficient significance and AICc.
- **Residual analysis:** portmanteau tests, white noise tests and spectral
  analysis.

We find that the SARIMA(0,1,3)(0,1,1)$_{12}$ model is the best candidate, and
that its residuals, forecasts and spectral decomposition support its use.
All analysis was performed in R.

## Data

### Description

The data are monthly measurements of atmospheric CO$_2$ above Mauna Loa from
January 1959 to December 1990, in parts per million (ppm). They were
collected by the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, La Jolla, California
and are available through the `tsdl` package [@hyndman2019]. Missing values
in the raw data were filled by linear interpolation. The raw series
$x_t,~t=1,\dots,384$ has 384 observations.

```{r}
#| label: setup
# libraries
library(tsdl)       # source for data
library(zoo)        # rollmean
library(ggplot2)    # plots and figures
library(tidyr)      # reshaping data
library(gridExtra)  # multiple ggplots
library(forecast)   # seasonal plot, Arima
library(tseries)    # adf and kpss tests
library(knitr)      # tables
library(astsa)      # acf2
library(LSTS)       # Ljung-Box plot
library(TSA)        # periodogram
library(ggpubr)     # qqplot
library(lmtest)     # coeftest
library(ggplottimeseries) # time series decomposition
# remotes::install_github("brisneve/ggplottimeseries")

theme_set(theme_minimal())
set.seed(8467)

# plot the roots of an AR / MA polynomial against the unit circle
plot.roots <- function(ar.roots = NULL, ma.roots = NULL, size = 2,
                       angles = FALSE, special = NULL, sqecial = NULL,
                       my.pch = 1, first.col = "blue", second.col = "red",
                       main = NULL) {
  xylims <- c(-size, size)
  omegas <- seq(0, 2 * pi, pi / 500)
  temp <- exp(complex(real = rep(0, length(omegas)), imag = omegas))
  plot(Re(temp), Im(temp), typ = "l", xlab = "x", ylab = "y",
       xlim = xylims, ylim = xylims, main = main)
  abline(v = 0, lty = "dotted")
  abline(h = 0, lty = "dotted")
  if (!is.null(ar.roots)) {
    points(Re(1 / ar.roots), Im(1 / ar.roots), col = first.col, pch = my.pch)
    points(Re(ar.roots), Im(ar.roots), col = second.col, pch = my.pch)
  }
  if (!is.null(ma.roots)) {
    points(Re(1 / ma.roots), Im(1 / ma.roots), pch = "*", cex = 1.5,
           col = first.col)
    points(Re(ma.roots), Im(ma.roots), pch = "*", cex = 1.5, col = second.col)
  }
  if (angles) {
    if (!is.null(ar.roots)) {
      abline(a = 0, b = Im(ar.roots[1]) / Re(ar.roots[1]), lty = "dotted")
      abline(a = 0, b = Im(ar.roots[2]) / Re(ar.roots[2]), lty = "dotted")
    }
    if (!is.null(ma.roots)) {
      sapply(seq_along(ma.roots), function(j)
        abline(a = 0, b = Im(ma.roots[j]) / Re(ma.roots[j]), lty = "dotted"))
    }
  }
  if (!is.null(special)) lines(Re(special), Im(special), lwd = 2)
  if (!is.null(sqecial)) lines(Re(sqecial), Im(sqecial), lwd = 2)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: data
# load the monthly CO2 series from the Time Series Data Library
tsdl_met <- subset(tsdl, 12, "Meteorology")
rawdata <- tsdl_met[[2]]
```

### Exploratory Analysis

We split the data into disjoint training and testing sets. The testing set
contains the last 5 years (60 months) of observed CO$_2$ and is used to assess
the forecasts of the final model. The training set contains 324 observations.

```{r}
#| label: split
data <- head(rawdata, n = length(rawdata) - (12 * 5))
```

@fig-raw shows the training data with a 12 month moving average. There is a
clear increasing polynomial trend and a seasonal component with a 12 month
period, so the raw data are non-stationary. The variance appears constant and
there are no sharp changes in behaviour, which suggests a SARIMA model should
suit the data.

```{r}
#| label: fig-raw
#| fig-cap: "Atmospheric carbon dioxide above Mauna Loa, Hawaii."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
# 12 month moving average
maline <- rollmean(data, k = 12, fill = NA, align = "right")

plotdata <- data.frame(
  "Time" = seq(as.Date("1959/1/1"), as.Date("1985/12/1"), "months"),
  "data" = data,
  "trend" = maline
)

plotdata %>%
  tidyr::gather("id", "value", 2:3) %>%
  ggplot(., aes(Time, value, col = id, linetype = id)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_light() +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "CO2 (ppm)", color = "Legend", linetype = "Legend")
```

The decomposition in @fig-decomp separates the seasonal and trend components.
There is no evidence of heteroscedastic behaviour in the residuals, so we do
not transform the data.

```{r}
#| label: fig-decomp
#| fig-cap: "Time series decomposition, seasonal plot and trend plot."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
ts_decomp <- ggdecompose(dts2(data, type = "additive")) +
  xlab("Date") +
  ylab("Atmospheric Concentration of CO2") +
  ggtitle("Time Series Decomposition Plots")
seasplot <- ggseasonplot(data, year.labels = TRUE, year.labels.left = TRUE) +
  ylab("CO2 (ppm)") +
  ggtitle("Seasonal plot") +
  theme_minimal()
trendplot <- autoplot(maline, ts.color = "red", main = "Trend plot") +
  theme_minimal()
grid.arrange(ts_decomp, seasplot, trendplot,
             layout_matrix = rbind(c(1, 1), c(2, 3)))
```

The autocorrelation function (ACF) in @fig-acf-raw shows highly significant
autocorrelations for all lags up to 40, which decay slowly and show
seasonality.

```{r}
#| label: fig-acf-raw
#| fig-cap: "ACF and PACF of the raw data."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| results: hide
acf2(data, 40, main = "ACF and PACF of raw data.")
```

### Differencing

We difference first with lag 12 to remove the seasonal component:

$$
y_t = x_t - x_{t-12} = (1-B^{12})x_t = \nabla_{12}x_t,
$$

where $B$ is the back-shift operator, $B^kx_t = x_{t-k}$. @fig-diff12 shows
that the seasonal pattern is gone but a linear trend remains, and the ACF
decays slowly as is typical of data with a polynomial trend.

```{r}
#| label: fig-diff12
#| fig-cap: "Time series and ACF of the seasonally differenced data."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5
data_d <- diff(data, 12)

plot_data_d <- data.frame(
  "Time" = seq(as.Date("1960/1/1"), as.Date("1985/12/1"), "months"),
  "yt" = data_d
)
tsplot_data_d <- plot_data_d %>%
  tidyr::gather("id", "value", 2:2) %>%
  ggplot(., aes(Time, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Seasonally Differenced Monthly CO2") +
  geom_smooth(method = lm)

acfplot_data_d <- autoplot(acf(data_d, lag = 40, plot = FALSE))

grid.arrange(tsplot_data_d, acfplot_data_d, ncol = 2)
```

We difference again with lag 1 to remove the linear trend:

$$
u_t = y_t - y_{t-1} = (1-B)y_t = (1-B)(1-B^{12})x_t = \nabla_1\nabla_{12}x_t.
$$

```{r}
#| label: fig-diff1
#| fig-cap: "Time series plot of the differenced and seasonally differenced data."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
data_dd <- diff(data_d, 1)

plot_data_dd <- data.frame(
  "Time" = seq(as.Date("1960/2/1"), as.Date("1985/12/1"), "months"),
  "yt" = data_dd
)
plot_data_dd %>%
  tidyr::gather("id", "value", 2:2) %>%
  ggplot(., aes(Time, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Transformed Data (ut)")
```

The twice differenced data appear stationary, with no seasonality or trend
and a stable variance. Each transformation lowered the variance of the data
(@tbl-var).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-var
#| tbl-cap: "Variance of the data after each transformation."
var_table <- data.frame(
  "Transformation" = c("None", "Differenced lag 12",
                       "Differenced lag 12 and lag 1"),
  "Variance" = c(var(data), var(data_d), var(data_dd))
)
kable(var_table)
```

The ACF, histogram and Q-Q plot in @fig-dd-diag show no remaining polynomial
or seasonal trend, and an empirical distribution that is symmetric and
approximately Gaussian.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dd-diag
#| fig-cap: "ACF, histogram and Q-Q plot of the twice differenced data."
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4
acf_data_dd <- autoplot(acf(data_dd, lag = 40, plot = FALSE))

hist_data_dd <- ggplot(data.frame("data" = data_dd), aes(x = data)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "darkblue", fill = "lightblue") +
  ggtitle("Histogram")

qqplot_data_dd <- ggqqplot(data_dd, color = "darkblue") + ggtitle("Q-Q plot")

grid.arrange(acf_data_dd, hist_data_dd, qqplot_data_dd, ncol = 3)
```

Finally, we run two stationarity tests. The Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test
has a unit root (and hence a trend) as its null, so a large p-value indicates
a trend. The Kwiatkowski-Phillips-Schmidt-Shin (KPSS) test has trend
stationarity as its null, so a small p-value indicates a unit root. Both
conclude that the twice differenced data are trend stationary (@tbl-stat).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-stat
#| tbl-cap: "Trend stationarity test results."
adf_test <- adf.test(data_dd)
kpss_test <- kpss.test(data_dd, null = "Trend")

table_data <- data.frame(
  Test = c("ADF Test", "KPSS Test"),
  Null = c("Process has a unit root and therefore a trend.",
           "Process is trend stationary"),
  pValue = c(signif(adf_test$p.value, 2), signif(kpss_test$p.value, 2)),
  Conclusion = c("Data is trend stationary", "Data is trend stationary")
)
kable(table_data)
```

## Model Fitting

### Parameter Selection

A SARIMA model has seven parameters: $p, d, q, P, D, Q$ and $s$. Since we
differenced once at lag 1 and once at lag 12, we have $d=1$, $D=1$ and
$s=12$. To bound the AR parameters $p, P$ and MA parameters $q, Q$ we inspect
the ACF and PACF of the differenced data (@fig-acf-dd).

```{r}
#| label: fig-acf-dd
#| fig-cap: "ACF and PACF of the transformed data."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| results: hide
acf2(data_dd, 60, main = "ACF and PACF of transformed data")
```

- **Non-seasonal AR ($p$):** the PACF has significant spikes at lags 1 and 3,
  so we may need up to $p=3$. Spikes at lags 9 and 11 are likely interactions
  with the seasonal terms.
- **Non-seasonal MA ($q$):** the ACF has significant spikes at lags 1 and 3,
  so we may need up to $q=3$.
- **Seasonal AR ($P$):** the PACF is significant at lags 12, 24 and 36, so we
  may need up to $P=3$.
- **Seasonal MA ($Q$):** the ACF is significant at lag 12 only, so we likely
  need $Q=1$.

### Model Selection

We fit, evaluate and compare models using the AICc. Since the AICc penalises
large numbers of parameters, we start from the simplest models and add
parameters with the aim of minimising the AICc. A full summary of every model
considered is given in the [appendix](#summary-of-fitted-models).

#### Pure Moving Average Models

We first fix $p=P=0$ and find the best pure moving average model, with up to
$q=3$ and $Q=1$. The two best models are below.

```{r}
#| label: ma-models
# SARIMA(0,1,3)(0,1,1)12
model1 <- Arima(data, order = c(0, 1, 3),
                seasonal = list(order = c(0, 1, 1), period = 12),
                method = "ML")
# SARIMA(0,1,3)(0,1,1)12 with MA2 = 0
model2 <- Arima(data, order = c(0, 1, 3),
                seasonal = list(order = c(0, 1, 1), period = 12),
                method = "ML", fix = c(NA, 0, NA, NA))
```

::: {#tbl-ma layout-ncol=2}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-ma-1
#| tbl-cap: "SARIMA(0,1,3)(0,1,1)$_{12}$"
kable(round(cbind(Est = model1$coef, SE = sqrt(diag(model1$var.coef)),
                  z = model1$coef / sqrt(diag(model1$var.coef)),
                  p = coeftest(model1)[, 4]), 4))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-ma-2
#| tbl-cap: "SARIMA(0,1,3)(0,1,1)$_{12}$ with MA2 = 0"
cf <- coeftest(model2)
kable(round(cf[, 1:4], 4))
```

Best pure moving average models. AICc: 119.57 (left), 117.51 (right).
:::

The MA(2) coefficient of the first model is insignificant, so we fix it to
zero and refit. This lowers the AICc from 119.57 to 117.51 and leaves all
coefficients significant, making it our top pure MA model.

#### Autoregressive Terms

We next test whether AR terms reduce the AICc by more than their penalty. The
two best candidates are below.

```{r}
#| label: ar-models
# SARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)12
modelB <- Arima(data, order = c(1, 1, 1),
                seasonal = list(order = c(0, 1, 1), period = 12),
                method = "ML")
# SARIMA(3,1,1)(0,1,1)12 with AR1 = AR2 = 0
armodel2 <- Arima(data, order = c(3, 1, 1),
                  seasonal = list(order = c(0, 1, 1), period = 12),
                  method = "ML", fixed = c(0, 0, NA, NA, NA))
```

::: {#tbl-ar layout-ncol=2}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-ar-1
#| tbl-cap: "SARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)$_{12}$"
kable(round(coeftest(modelB)[, 1:4], 4))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-ar-2
#| tbl-cap: "SARIMA(3,1,1)(0,1,1)$_{12}$ with AR1 = AR2 = 0"
kable(round(coeftest(armodel2)[, 1:4], 4))
```

Best models with autoregressive terms. AICc: 123.37 (left), 119.96 (right).
:::

Adding seasonal AR terms typically increased the AICc and rarely gave
significant coefficients. The SARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)$_{12}$ model performs
reasonably well, with all coefficients significant and an AICc of 123.37. The
SARIMA(3,1,1)(0,1,1)$_{12}$ model with AR1 = AR2 = 0 has the second best AICc
(119.96) but is not viable, since the absolute value of its seasonal MA
coefficient is greater than 1. We therefore take the SARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)$_{12}$
model as our second candidate.

The two candidates are:

**Model (A)**

$$
\nabla_1\nabla_{12}X_t=(1-0.354998_{(0.053140)}B-0.155974_{(0.052126)}B^3)
(1-0.838438_{(0.035989)}B^{12})Z_t,\quad \hat\sigma_Z^2=0.08431
$$

**Model (B)**

$$
\nabla_1\nabla_{12}(1-0.344624_{(0.151353)}B)X_t=
(1-0.675336_{(0.123186)}B)(1-0.839105_{(0.035565)}B^{12})Z_t,\quad
\hat\sigma_Z^2=0.08583
$$

where $Z_t$ is white noise (WN) with $\mathbb{E}Z_t=0$ and
$\operatorname{Var}(Z_t)=\sigma_Z^2$.

Model (A) is pure moving average, so it is always stationary. In
@fig-roots all MA roots lie outside the unit circle and $|\Theta_1|<1$, so
the model is invertible. Model (B) is invertible since $|\theta_1|<1$ and
$|\Theta_1|<1$, and stationary since $|\phi_1|<1$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-roots
#| fig-cap: "Model (A): roots of the non-seasonal MA polynomial."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5
# final models
finalmodel1 <- Arima(data, order = c(0, 1, 3),
                     seasonal = list(order = c(0, 1, 1), period = 12),
                     method = "ML", fix = c(NA, 0, NA, NA))
finalmodel2 <- Arima(data, order = c(1, 1, 1),
                     seasonal = list(order = c(0, 1, 1), period = 12),
                     method = "ML", fixed = c(NA, NA, NA))

plot.roots(NULL, polyroot(c(1, 0.354998, 0, -0.155974)),
           main = "Roots of the non-seasonal MA part")
```

## Diagnostic Checking

For each candidate we plot the residuals alongside their ACF, PACF, histogram,
Q-Q plot and Ljung-Box statistics, then run a set of residual tests. The
helper below builds both for a fitted model.

```{r}
#| label: diag-helpers
# residual diagnostic plots for a fitted model
resid_plots <- function(fit) {
  r <- fit$residuals
  grid.arrange(
    autoplot(r, ylab = "Residuals"),
    autoplot(acf(r, plot = FALSE)) + ggtitle("ACF plot"),
    ggplot(data.frame("data" = r), aes(x = data)) +
      geom_histogram(color = "darkblue", fill = "lightblue") +
      ggtitle("Histogram"),
    autoplot(pacf(r, plot = FALSE)) + ggtitle("PACF plot"),
    ggqqplot(r, color = "darkblue") + ggtitle("Q-Q plot"),
    Box.Ljung.Test(r, lag = 30),
    layout_matrix = rbind(c(1, 1), c(2, 3), c(4, 5), c(6, 6))
  )
}

# residual tests for a fitted model
resid_tests <- function(fit) {
  r <- fit$residuals
  sw <- shapiro.test(r)
  bp <- Box.test(r, lag = 18, type = "Box-Pierce", fitdf = 3)
  lb <- Box.test(r, lag = 18, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 3)
  lbs <- Box.test(r^2, lag = 18, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 0)
  data.frame(
    "Test" = c("Shapiro-Wilk", "Box-Pierce", "Ljung-Box",
               "Ljung-Box (squared)"),
    "p-value" = c(sw$p.value, bp$p.value, lb$p.value, lbs$p.value),
    "Conclusion" = c("Normal", "Independence",
                     "No autocorrelation in residuals",
                     "No autocorrelation in squared residuals")
  )
}
```

### Model (A)

```{r}
#| label: fig-resid-a
#| fig-cap: "Model (A): residual analysis plots."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 9
resid_plots(finalmodel1)
```

The residuals show the characteristics of white noise, with no trend,
seasonality or conditional heteroscedasticity. The ACF and PACF show no
significant spikes up to lag 25, apart from a borderline spike at lag 9. Bar a
lower outlier, the histogram and Q-Q plot are consistent with a Gaussian
distribution. The Ljung-Box p-values are not significant at any lag up to 30.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-resid-a
#| tbl-cap: "Model (A): residual test results."
kable(resid_tests(finalmodel1))
```

Model (A) passes all four tests.

### Model (B)

```{r}
#| label: fig-resid-b
#| fig-cap: "Model (B): residual analysis plots."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 9
resid_plots(finalmodel2)
```

The residual behaviour is similar, with borderline spikes at lags 2 and 9 and
a slightly heavier tailed distribution than Model (A). No Ljung-Box p-values
are significant, but they are much closer to the rejection region than for
Model (A).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-resid-b
#| tbl-cap: "Model (B): residual test results."
kable(resid_tests(finalmodel2))
```

Model (B) also passes all four tests.

Both models pass diagnostic checking. Because of the slight edge in the
residual analysis of Model (A) and its lower AICc, we select Model (A) as the
final model. It is also simpler than our initial speculation from the ACF and
PACF, so the AICc procedure kept the model parsimonious.

## Forecasting

Our final model is the SARIMA(0,1,3)(0,1,1)$_{12}$ model with the MA2
coefficient fixed at 0:

$$
\nabla_1\nabla_{12}X_t=(1-0.354998_{(0.053140)}B-0.155974_{(0.052126)}B^3)
(1-0.838438_{(0.035989)}B^{12})Z_t,\quad \hat\sigma_Z^2=0.08431
$$

We produce a 5 year (60 month) ahead forecast with approximate 95%
prediction bounds (@fig-forecast).

```{r}
#| label: fig-forecast
#| fig-cap: "60 month forecast of atmospheric CO2 above Mauna Loa, Hawaii."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6
pred.tr <- predict(finalmodel1, n.ahead = 60)
U.tr <- pred.tr$pred + 2 * pred.tr$se  # upper prediction bound
L.tr <- pred.tr$pred - 2 * pred.tr$se  # lower prediction bound
fc_time <- seq(time(rawdata)[length(rawdata) - 59],
               time(rawdata)[length(rawdata)], by = (1 / 12))

plot(data, xlim = c(time(data)[1], time(rawdata)[length(rawdata)]),
     ylim = c(min(data), max(U.tr)), ylab = "CO2 (ppm)")
lines(U.tr, col = "blue", lty = "dashed")
lines(L.tr, col = "blue", lty = "dashed")
lines(fc_time, pred.tr$pred, col = "red")
legend("topleft", legend = c("Forecast", "Confidence Bounds"),
       col = c("red", "blue"), lty = c(1, 2))
```

@fig-forecast-zoom focuses on the period since 1980 and overlays the true
observed values from the testing set.

```{r}
#| label: fig-forecast-zoom
#| fig-cap: "Forecast with the observed test data overlaid."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6
plot(data,
     xlim = c(time(data)[length(rawdata) - 130], time(rawdata)[length(rawdata)]),
     ylim = c(330, max(U.tr)), ylab = "CO2 (ppm)")
lines(U.tr, col = "blue", lty = "dashed")
lines(L.tr, col = "blue", lty = "dashed")
lines(fc_time, pred.tr$pred, col = "red")
points(fc_time, rawdata[(length(rawdata) - 59):length(rawdata)], pch = 20)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Forecast", "Confidence Bounds",
                             "Observed Values"),
       col = c("red", "blue", "black"), lty = c(1, 2, NA),
       pch = c(NA, NA, 20))
```

The forecast was successful. The observed values lie inside the confidence
region throughout the five year window. Between 1988 and 1990 the forecast
lags below the observed values, which approach the upper bound before
returning close to the forecast by the end of 1990. Despite the large (and
somewhat impractical) forecasting window, the forecast was accurate.

## Spectral Analysis

We first compute periodograms of the undifferenced data and of the residuals
of the final model (@fig-periodogram).

```{r}
#| label: fig-periodogram
#| fig-cap: "Periodograms of the data (left) and the final model residuals (right)."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5
#| results: hide
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
periodogram(data)
periodogram(finalmodel1$residuals)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The periodogram of the data has a spike near $0.08\approx 1/12$, matching the
12 month period seen in the seasonal plot. The periodogram of the residuals
has no dominant frequency, so no significant seasonality remains.

Fisher's test detects hidden periodicities of unspecified frequency in the
residuals. Its null hypothesis is Gaussian white noise.

```{r}
#| label: fisher
library(GeneCycle)
fisher.g.test(as.numeric(finalmodel1$residuals))
```

The p-value is above 0.05, so there is insufficient evidence to reject
Gaussian white noise. A second test is the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, which we
apply through the cumulative periodogram of the residuals (@fig-cpgram). The
cumulative periodogram stays inside the confidence band for all frequencies,
so the residuals pass this test too.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cpgram
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative periodogram of the final model residuals."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
cpgram(finalmodel1$residuals, main = "")
```

## Conclusion

We determined and fitted a model that gives accurate forecasts of monthly
atmospheric CO$_2$ above Mauna Loa, Hawaii (January 1959 to December 1990).
Exploratory analysis revealed a linear trend and a 12 month seasonal pattern,
both removed by differencing. We fitted a range of SARIMA models and chose
the best by AICc and then by residual analysis. The final model is the
SARIMA(0,1,3)(0,1,1)$_{12}$ model with MA2 fixed at 0.

Its 60 month forecast contained all future observations within the confidence
region. Spectral analysis supports the choice, with residuals that are
consistent with Gaussian white noise and no remaining seasonality.
